title: How Snails Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore snails: their biology and body plan (shell, epiphragm, torsion, mantle, pneumostome breathing, mucus trail), the torsion evolution debate, hermaphroditic mating and love darts, lifespan and reproduction, their ecological role as decomposers and pollinators, invasive species (giant African land snail, rosy wolf snail, common garden snail) and garden pest control, snail-related oddities (escargot, white caviar, Alzheimer's research with pond snails, medieval snail-fighting knight manuscripts), followed by a listener mail correction about isotopes versus ions.

entities.name: The Strange and Wonderful World of the Snail Wrangler

segments.title: Live show tour announcement
segments.summary: Hosts promote upcoming live shows in Seattle, Portland, and San Francisco (Sketchfest) in January and where to buy tickets.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Opening banter about a song by Tom Cochrane and the hosts' chatter about the episode topic.

segments.title: Choosing the snail topic
segments.summary: Josh explains the snail topic was his pick, notes limited academic information on snails and gardener folklore, and malacology is the study of mollusks.

segments.title: Gastropods and snail diversity
segments.summary: Snails belong to the class Gastropoda within phylum Mollusca; there are roughly 30,000 to 35,000 snail species, from giant African land snails to tiny cave snails; about 500 native North American species; and more than 400 recorded snail extinctions.

segments.title: Snail eating and escargot
segments.summary: Discussion of eating snails, serving plates for escargot, and snail caviar (white caviar).

segments.title: Snail shell and epiphragm
segments.summary: The shell is protective; snails can seal the opening with a temporary epiphragm; some shells have denticles; the shell keeps moisture in.

segments.title: Snail body arrangement and torsion
segments.summary: The snail's foot is what appears as the tail, the body is inside the shell, and the head and anus sit near the aperture because the body twists during development (torsion). Scientists are unsure when torsion emerged; the rotational and asymmetrical hypotheses are the main competing explanations.

segments.title: The torsion debate
segments.summary: Describes the rotational hypothesis (since 1929) and the asymmetry hypothesis, with the body twisting counterclockwise during larval development and the right-side organs shifted to the left.

segments.title: Eyes, tentacles, and senses
segments.summary: Snails have no ears but have eyes on tentacles that they can retract into the shell; eye simplicity varies by species.

segments.title: Mantle and shell formation
segments.summary: The mantle secretes calcium carbonate that builds the shell; the oldest part is in the center and hardest; snails are born with a starter shell.

segments.title: Breathing through the pneumostome
segments.summary: Land snails breathe through a lung-like opening (pneumostome) near the head at the aperture.

segments.title: Snail mucus
segments.summary: Mucus from the foot acts as glue or lubricant, lets snails climb walls, protects from sharp objects, and keeps moisture; snail mucin is used in skin products.

segments.title: Snail mating and love darts
segments.summary: Most land snails are hermaphroditic; they court for hours, bite lips, and shoot or stab with love darts that deliver hormones; both can be fertilized; eggs hatch in two to four weeks; hatchlings may eat eggs.

segments.title: Snail lifespan and snail wranglers
segments.summary: Snails live up to five years in the wild and up to 25 in captivity; a documentary about a snail wrangler is mentioned.

segments.title: Snails and dry land survival and ecology
segments.summary: Snails are moisture-dependent and mostly active at night; they act as decomposers, recycle nutrients, aid drainage, and some are nighttime pollinators.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Snails as garden pests and control methods
segments.summary: Burgundy snails eat plants; gardeners' control methods include beetles, handpicking, compost traps, and pesticides like ferric phosphate and metaldehyde, which is banned in the EU.

segments.title: Giant African land snail
segments.summary: The giant African land snail is invasive in North America, eats many plant species, can carry rat lungworm and meningitis, and is kept illegally as a pet.

segments.title: Rosy wolf snail and Hawaii
segments.summary: Rosy wolf snails were introduced in the 1950s in Hawaii to control giant African land snails, but they preyed on native snails, causing losses; a malacologist found thirteen snail shells in one wolf snail's gut.

segments.title: Common garden snail as invasive
segments.summary: The common garden snail is considered invasive in the United States; it was imported for escargot and spread from farms.

segments.title: Snail factoids: jewelry, Patricia Highsmith, Alzheimer's, and religion
segments.summary: Snail shells used as jewelry over 120,000 years ago; author Patricia Highsmith kept snails; pond snails used in amyloid beta Alzheimer's research; common garden snail mucus shows bioactive properties; giant African land snail sacred in Yoruba religion.

segments.title: Snail recipe and medieval snail-fighting knights
segments.summary: A Nigerian snail recipe is mentioned; medieval illuminated manuscripts from late thirteenth-century northern France show knights fighting giant snails, with theories about comic relief or symbolism.

segments.title: Listener mail: isotope correction
segments.summary: Listener Nick Lufti corrects the hosts: isotopes differ by neutron count, while losing or gaining an electron makes an ion.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener email and close the show.
